title: Complex Subordinate Clauses
subtitle: Link ideas with precision using concessive, purpose and result clauses.
objectives: Use concessive clauses (even though, whereas, despite/in spite of) to show contrast
Use purpose clauses (so as to, in order to/that) to explain why something is done
Use result clauses (so...that, such...that) to show the consequence of a degree or quality
Choose the right register for each connector in formal writing versus speech

content.intro: Subordinate clauses let you link a main idea to a secondary one with precision. At C1 you need to control three families beyond simple “because” / “although”.

rules.heading: a) Concessive clauses (contrast)
rules.body:
even though, although, though, whereas, while, in spite of / despite (+ noun or -ing)

  • “Even though / although / though” + clause show a surprising contrast: Even though it was raining, we went for a walk.
  • “Whereas / while” contrast two facts neutrally, often side by side: She loves cities, whereas he prefers the countryside.
  • “In spite of / despite” + noun/gerund (never a full clause directly): Despite the rain, we went for a walk. / Despite working hard, she failed.

rules.heading: b) Purpose clauses
rules.body:
so as to, in order to/that, for the purpose of

  • “So as to” / “in order to” + bare infinitive express purpose formally: We left early so as to avoid the traffic.
  • “In order that” / “so that” + clause (with can/could/will/would) are used when the subject changes: I gave her my number so that she could contact me.

rules.heading: c) Result clauses
rules.body:
such...that, so...that

  • “So” + adjective/adverb + “that”: The exam was so difficult that half the class failed.
  • “Such” + (a/an) + adjective + noun + “that”: It was such a difficult exam that half the class failed.

content.registerNote: “In order that,” “so as to,” and “whereas” belong to formal/written English; “so,” “although,” and “but” are fine in speech.
examples: Even though she was exhausted, she finished the marathon.
Whereas the north of the country is mountainous, the south is flat.
Despite having no experience, he got the job.
In spite of the criticism, the director refused to change the ending.
We arrived early so as to get good seats.
She whispered so that no one else would hear.
He studied hard in order to pass the bar exam.
The music was so loud that we couldn't hear each other talk.
It was such a compelling argument that the jury changed its mind.
While I understand your concerns, I still disagree with the decision.
The report was so poorly written that it had to be redone.
He left the company in order that his rival could take over.

commonMistakes.wrong: Despite he was tired, he kept working.
commonMistakes.right: Despite being tired, he kept working. / Although he was tired, he kept working.
commonMistakes.why: “Despite/in spite of” take a noun or gerund, not a subject + verb clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: The film was such interesting that I watched it twice.
commonMistakes.right: The film was so interesting that I watched it twice.
commonMistakes.why: “So” goes with an adjective alone; “such” needs a noun (such an interesting film).

commonMistakes.wrong: She works hard so as she can support her family.
commonMistakes.right: She works hard so that she can support her family. / She works hard in order to support her family.
commonMistakes.why: “So as to” takes an infinitive, not a clause; use “so that” for a full clause with a modal.

commonMistakes.wrong: Whereas he is generous, but she is quite mean.
commonMistakes.right: Whereas he is generous, she is quite mean.
commonMistakes.why: Don't combine “whereas” with “but” — the contrast is already built into “whereas.”

commonMistakes.wrong: It was so a boring lecture that half the room fell asleep.
commonMistakes.right: It was such a boring lecture that half the room fell asleep.

exercises.title: Gap-fill
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with so, such, whereas, despite, in order to/that, or so as to.

items.prompt: ___ the traffic, we arrived right on time.
items.explanation: “Despite/in spite of” + noun expresses contrast without a full clause.

items.prompt: He whispered the plan ___ no one would overhear.
items.explanation: “So that” + clause expresses purpose when the subject can take a modal (would).

items.prompt: It was ___ a long meeting that people started checking their phones.
items.explanation: “Such” + a + adjective + noun + “that” for a result clause with a noun.

items.prompt: The coffee here is excellent, ___ the tea is rather weak.
items.explanation: “Whereas” neutrally contrasts two facts side by side.

items.prompt: She left the party early ___ catch the last train.
items.explanation: “So as to” / “in order to” + bare infinitive express purpose formally.

items.prompt: The instructions were ___ confusing that nobody followed them correctly.
items.explanation: “So” + adjective alone + “that” for a result clause without a noun.

items.prompt: He trained every day ___ improve his stamina.
items.explanation: Purpose clause with a bare infinitive.

items.prompt: ___ having a fever, she still went to work.
items.explanation: “Despite/in spite of” + gerund expresses contrast.

items.prompt: He spoke slowly and clearly ___ everyone in the room could understand.
items.explanation: “So that” + clause with a modal (could) for purpose.

items.prompt: It was ___ a generous offer that we couldn't refuse it.
items.explanation: “Such” + a + adjective + noun + “that” for a result clause with a noun.

exercises.title: Rewrite / Transformation
exercises.instructions: Rewrite each pair of sentences as one, using the connector given.

items.prompt: He is rich, but he lives very simply. (rewrite with “whereas”)
answer: He is rich, whereas he lives very simply.
items.explanation: “Whereas” replaces “but” to contrast the two facts formally.

items.prompt: She failed the exam, but she didn't lose confidence. (rewrite with “even though”)
answer: Even though she failed the exam, she didn't lose confidence.
items.explanation: “Even though” opens the clause with the surprising fact.

items.prompt: He turned down the promotion. He wanted more free time. (join with “in order to”)
answer: He turned down the promotion in order to have more free time.
items.explanation: “In order to” + bare infinitive expresses his purpose.

items.prompt: It rained heavily. We still finished the hike. (join with “despite”)
answer: Despite the heavy rain, we still finished the hike.
items.explanation: “Despite” + noun phrase replaces the first sentence.

items.prompt: The test was extremely hard. Nobody finished it in time. (join with “so...that”)
answer: The test was so hard that nobody finished it in time.
items.explanation: “So” + adjective + “that” shows the result of the degree.

items.prompt: He apologized publicly. He wanted to repair his reputation. (join with “so that”)
answer: He apologized publicly so that he could repair his reputation.
items.explanation: “So that” + clause with “could” expresses his purpose.

items.prompt: It was a very persuasive speech. It changed several votes. (join with “such...that”)
answer: It was such a persuasive speech that it changed several votes.
items.explanation: “Such” + a + adjective + noun + “that” shows the result.

items.incorrect: Despite he arrived late, no one seemed to mind.
answer: Despite arriving late, no one seemed to mind.
Although he arrived late, no one seemed to mind.
items.explanation: “Despite” needs a noun/gerund, not a subject + verb clause — use “although” if you want a full clause.

items.incorrect: It was so an emotional film that everyone cried.
answer: It was such an emotional film that everyone cried.
items.explanation: “Adjective + noun” needs “such (a/an),” not “so.”

items.incorrect: She practiced every day so as she could improve faster.
answer: She practiced every day so as to improve faster.
She practiced every day so that she could improve faster.
items.explanation: “So as to” takes an infinitive, not a clause; use “so that” for a full clause.

items.incorrect: Whereas I respect his opinion, but I think he's wrong.
answer: Whereas I respect his opinion, I think he's wrong.
items.explanation: Don't combine “whereas” with “but” — the contrast is already built into “whereas.”

items.incorrect: The meeting was such long that we had to order dinner.
answer: The meeting was so long that we had to order dinner.
items.explanation: “So” goes with an adjective alone; there's no noun here.

items.incorrect: In spite of he lost the match, he stayed positive.
answer: In spite of losing the match, he stayed positive.
Although he lost the match, he stayed positive.
items.explanation: “In spite of” needs a noun/gerund, not a subject + verb clause.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence for each prompt. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence about your own life using “even though.”
items.modelAnswer: Even though I was scared of heights, I went skydiving for my birthday.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “whereas” to contrast two people or places you know.
items.modelAnswer: My sister loves spontaneous trips, whereas I prefer planning every detail in advance.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “so...that” describing a memorable experience.
items.modelAnswer: The concert was so loud that my ears were ringing for hours afterward.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “in order to” about a goal you're working toward.
items.modelAnswer: I've been saving money in order to travel around South America next year.

summary: Concessive clauses (even though, whereas, despite/in spite of) show contrast — despite/in spite of take a noun or -ing, never a full clause.
Purpose clauses (so as to, in order to/that) explain why — so as to/in order to take an infinitive; so that/in order that take a clause with a modal.
Result clauses use so + adjective + that, or such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that.
In order that, so as to and whereas are formal/written; so, although and but are fine in speech.
